cards.front: Does a final class mean its objects are immutable?
cards.back: No — final only blocks subclassing; the fields can still be changed through setters
cards.extra: Immutability needs final fields plus no mutators. A final class with a setter is perfectly mutable.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.back: So nobody can subclass it and override its methods, which would make behaviour unpredictable across the whole language
cards.extra: Strings are passed everywhere and used as map keys; a subclass with altered equals or hashCode would break collections invisibly.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.back: Overriding it in a subclass — the method body is fixed
cards.extra: The class can still be extended and new methods added; only that method is locked.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: What is the difference between making every method final and making the class final?
cards.back: With final methods you can still subclass and add methods; with a final class you cannot subclass at all
cards.extra: The first restricts behaviour, the second restricts the type hierarchy.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: When should you mark a method final even in an extensible class?
cards.back: When other methods or the constructor call it — an override would silently change the caller's behaviour
cards.extra: This is why Thread is extensible but isAlive() is final: its contract cannot be reimplemented safely.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: What does final mean on a reference variable?
cards.back: The reference cannot be reassigned; the object it points at stays fully mutable
cards.extra: final List<String> l = new ArrayList<>(); still allows l.add(...) — only l = other is forbidden.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: When must a final instance field be assigned?
cards.back: Before the constructor completes — at declaration, in an instance initializer block, or in the constructor
cards.extra: That is what makes a final field safely published. Assigning it twice, or not at all, is a compile error.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: Where can a static final field be assigned?
cards.back: At declaration or in a static initializer block
cards.extra: Not in a constructor — a static field belongs to the class, which is initialised once regardless of how many objects are made.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: What does final on a method parameter do?
cards.back: Forbids reassigning the parameter inside the method body
cards.extra: It documents that the argument is not modified. The caller sees no difference; it is a local guarantee only.
cards.source: baeldung.com — The final Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword
